summary:
Jordan does not criminalise same-sex relations. The historic-era ban was abolished by the 1951 Penal Code, which legalised private, adult, consensual same-sex acts with an age of consent of 18 regardless of gender or orientation. No statute on the books prohibits gender expression as such, and the 1951 reform left no anti-discrimination protection in its place.

That baseline does not translate into safety. Human Rights Watch reported on 6 June 2024 that authorities in Jordan, Egypt and Kuwait substitute public-morality and debauchery provisions for formal criminalisation, using them to harass LGBT people. Vague morality provisions give security forces and private individuals licence to target LGBT people with impunity, and Human Rights Watch found Jordan's cybercrime and morality laws being used to persecute them.

Legal gender recognition has no clear pathway. Intersex people can change official gender markers; transgender people cannot. OutRight International records that marker changes are allowed in some cases without any defined procedure being published.

Gender-affirming surgery turns on intersex status. Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law (25) of 2018 permits such procedures for intersex people and criminalises them for transgender people, with CAIRO 52 recording penalties of up to 10 years' imprisonment for sex reassignment except in intersex cases. The same 2018 law outlaws changing of sex while permitting correction of sex, wording that also exposes doctors who perform gender-affirming surgery to medical-liability penalties.

In Case No. 2092/2014 the Court of Cassation allowed a plaintiff born in 1977 to change name and gender from male to female in official records after hormone therapy and surgery undertaken in Australia, since such procedures are unavailable domestically. The court justified the change by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex rather than transgender.

Speech and digital access are restricted. A cybercrime law promulgated in August 2023 can target digital content on gender and sexuality as well as activists advocating LGBT rights. Human Rights Watch reported on 11 January 2024 that the authorities limited civic space during 2023 and enacted a new cybercrime law undermining free speech and privacy online, with peaceful dissidents and journalists arrested and harassed under vague, abusive laws and intrusive digital surveillance applied. The Press and Publication Law, amended in 1998 and 2004, replaced a ban on depicting sexual perversion with a requirement that the press respect the values of the Arab and Islamic nation.

Security forces coerced queer community spaces into closing, pushing transgender and queer people to leave. On 4 December 2023 Human Rights Watch reported that Jordanian authorities systematically targeted LGBT rights activists in a coordinated crackdown on free expression and assembly around gender and sexuality. Officials smeared activists online by sexual orientation, social-media users posted their photographs alongside messages inciting violence, and two LGBT organisation directors cited official intimidation; several organisations shut down, suspended activities or their staff fled.
tangentialFactors:
Public hostility is high and measurable. A 2019 Arab Barometer survey found that 93% of Jordanians said society should not accept homosexuality, a level of social sanction that operates alongside, and independently of, the legal position.

Human Rights Watch's April 2018 report Audacity in Adversity documents LGBT activism across the Middle East and North Africa despite state-sponsored repression and stigma, and its annex lists the laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across the region, including Jordan. The same organisation groups Jordan with Egypt and Kuwait as states where alternative legal avenues substitute for formal criminalisation.

The 2013 revised Penal Code made the use of honour as a legal justification for murder illegal, removing a defence that had previously operated against women and gender-nonconforming people in domestic violence cases.

CAIRO 52's Jordan profile records new legislation curtailing LGBTQ speech and digital access, a restriction that sits alongside the cybercrime and press laws rather than replacing them.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the same morality and cybercrime provisions described for visitors, and the 1951 decriminalisation conferred no protective status: the absence of a sodomy offence has never been paired with anti-discrimination or hate-crime legislation.

A small number of cafés in Amman are tolerated and widely considered gay-friendly. Books@Cafe, opened in 1997, remains a popular bookstore and café for patrons supportive of creativity, diversity and tolerance.

My.Kali, the first LGBTQ publication in the region, launched in 2007 and has been online since 2008, operating under the press restrictions that followed the 1998 and 2004 amendments to the Press and Publication Law.

Transgender Jordanians cannot obtain a marker change and face criminal exposure for gender-affirming surgery, while intersex Jordanians can change markers and access such procedures lawfully. Providers are exposed to liability under the 2018 medical law, and hormone therapy and surgery are unavailable domestically, which is why the plaintiff in Case No. 2092/2014 sought treatment in Australia.

Civic space narrowed sharply in 2023: dissidents and journalists were arrested and harassed, digital surveillance was intrusive, and LGBT organisations suspended their work or closed.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Case No. 2092/2014 establishes a binding precedent for transgender marker changes, or remains a one-off decision routed through an intersex reclassification, is unresolved in the sources available here.

The figure of up to 10 years' imprisonment for sex reassignment comes from CAIRO 52's analysis of the case; the operative statutory text and article number behind that penalty were not independently verified in this inventory, and the sources do not reconcile it with Article 8 of the 2018 medical-liability law.

OutRight International's statement that marker changes are allowed in some cases is not accompanied by a description of the procedure, the deciding authority, or the criteria applied.

The relationship between the cybercrime law promulgated in August 2023 and the new cybercrime law described by Human Rights Watch in January 2024 is not resolved here; they may be the same instrument or successive ones.

CAIRO 52 refers to new legislation curtailing LGBTQ speech and digital access without naming the instruments in the material supplied, so the specific statutes behind that claim remain unverified.
